1.note: Edinah (עֲדִינָה, "the pampered one") is what Isa 47:8 calls Babylon. In this gate it stands for the chief city of Iraq, most probably Baghdad; it is named again near the end, in the tour of Iraq.

2.note: Elam, the biblical name for the land east of Babylonia, in medieval Hebrew usually Persia (western Iran).

3.note: Ezek 1:16 "the appearance of the wheels and their work". אוֹפַנִּים "wheels" also sounds like אֳפָנִים "manners, ways": Heman asks to hear what the people are like and what they do.

4.note: Prov 7:17 מֹר אֲהָלִים "myrrh and aloes"; אֲהָלִים "aloes" is spelled like אֹהָלִים "tents", so the line plays "aloes from among its tents".

5.note: Meir ben Todros ha-Levi Abulafia of Toledo (died 1244), Talmudist and opponent of Maimonides' views on resurrection.

6.note: Sheshet Benveniste of Barcelona (died about 1209), physician, poet and patron, a defender of Maimonides.

7.note: בַּלְקִירִי is read as Beaucaire on the Rhône, in Provence, between Narbonne and Marseille on the route. The identification is probable, not certain.

8.note: A pun: he is of the Karaites (קָרָאִים, qara'im) and head of the "called" (קְרוּאִים, qeru'im), the notables of the assembly (compare Num 1:16).

9.note: Zoan (Num 13:22, Isa 19:11), the old royal city of Egypt. Here it is Cairo, the seat of the Ayyubid sultan. The "second city", where Abraham son of Maimonides lived, is Fustat (Old Cairo).

10.note: His work: the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides' code of Talmudic law, which gives the rulings without the names of the sages and without the Talmud's debate.

11.note: "The Land of the Gazelle" (Dan 11:16, 11:41) is the Land of Israel; Shinar (Gen 11:2) is Babylonia, that is, Iraq.

12.he: הָרַב הֶחָסִיד רַבִּי יוֹסֵף בֶּן הָרַב רַבִּי בָרוּךְ
12.note: Joseph ben Barukh and his brother Meir, Tosafists who went from France to the Land of Israel in the emigration of 1211.

13.note: "Head of the academy Pride of Jacob" (Ps 47:5) is the formal title of a Gaon, head of one of the great academies. The next lines tell that Zadok lost the office and went into exile.

14.note: Josiah son of Jesse, Nasi of Damascus, the patron to whom the book is dedicated in gate 1.

15.note: A pun: קְדוֹשִׁים (qedoshim) "holy ones" and קְדֵשִׁים (qedeshim) "cult prostitutes" (Deut 23:18, 1 Kgs 14:24) differ by one vowel.

16.note: The name Barukh means "blessed"; the satire calls him "accursed" and sets him on Mount Ebal, the mountain of the curses (Deut 27:13).

17.note: Gen 34:8 "And Hamor spoke with them, saying". The name Hamor means "donkey"; the verse prepares the joke below, where the son is named "Shechem son of Hamor". "Fathers of impurity" is the legal term for the main sources of ritual impurity (m. Kelim 1).

18.note: A rhyming title, perhaps an honorific of the Arabic kind ("Crown of ..."): כֶּתֶר הַמְּאוֹרוֹת (keter ha-me'orot) "crown of the lights" is turned into יֶתֶר הַמְּאֵרוֹת (yeter ha-me'erot) "the rest of the curses" by a change of one letter and one vowel.

19.note: Shechem son of Hamor, who violated Dinah (Gen 34:2); the name means "son of a donkey", since the father is as stupid as an ox and a donkey. Below, Shechem "violates" the poet's poem in the same words.

20.note: Num 32:42 "and he called it Nobah, after his own name". נֹבַח (Nobah) is read as נוֹבֵחַ "barking": he barks his poems and names his poetry "Barking".

21.he: שִׁירָתוֹ קְדֵשָׁה. / לֹא קְדוֹשָׁה. / וּמְחֻלֶּלֶת. / לֹא מְהֻלֶּלֶת
21.note: Two puns: קְדֵשָׁה "harlot" and קְדוֹשָׁה "holy"; מְחֻלֶּלֶת "profaned" and מְהֻלֶּלֶת "praised". The lines after this treat the poetry as Tamar at the entrance to Enaim (Gen 38).

22.note: Gen 38:15, Judah and Tamar. Judah is also the author's own name, Judah al-Ḥarizi, who in the next lines tells how he sent this man a poem.

23.he: לֶחֶם מַצָּה בְּלִי חָמֵץ. / וְהַיַּיִן חֹמֶץ
23.note: A pun that cannot be carried over: the bread is without חָמֵץ (ḥamets, leaven), and the wine is חֹמֶץ (ḥomets, vinegar), the same letters.

24.note: Exod 25:33 "cups shaped like almonds on one branch (קָנֶה)" of the lampstand. Here the branch is the "branch of contempt" (בּוּז); the sense of the joke is uncertain.

25.he: אֶת הֶחָצִיר וְאֶת הַבְּצָלִים וְאֶת הַשּׁוּמִים
25.note: Num 11:5. חָצִיר means "leeks" in that verse, but "grass" elsewhere, as in the lines above ("pots full of grass", "all flesh is grass"). Both senses are meant.

26.note: A pun: גְּנוּת "disgrace" has the same letters as גַּנּוֹת "gardens", the word of the verse quoted two lines below (Isa 66:17), which speaks of idolatrous rites in gardens.

27.note: Hermon is the mountain of dew (Ps 133:3); the mountains of Gilboa were cursed to have no dew or rain (2 Sam 1:21). At his touch even Hermon would be so dry that Gilboa would envy it.

28.note: Mount Zemaraim (2 Chr 13:4; compare "the Zemarite", Gen 10:18). On the route between Damascus and Hamath it is probably Homs (Ḥimṣ); the identification is not certain.

29.he: רַבִּי שְׁאֵרִית. / הוּא לַיּשֶׁר פְּלֵיטָה וּשְׁאֵרִית
29.note: The name She'erit means "remnant", hence the play "a survivor and a remnant" (compare Gen 45:7).

30.note: Hamath, the biblical name of Hama on the Orontes, in Syria.

31.note: Uncertain. מַפְגִּיעַ is from הִפְגִּיעַ "entreat, intercede" (Isa 53:12, Jer 36:25). Read as a wish that God command the redemption for Uzziel's sake; perhaps "and may He command it at his entreaty".

32.note: Gen 26:22: Isaac named the well Rehoboth, "for now the Lord has made room (הִרְחִיב) for us". The first half of the line quotes the same verse.

33.note: Num 11:28, said of Joshua, "the minister of Moses from his youth". Which Moses this Isaac served is not stated.

34.note: Aram Zobah (2 Sam 8:3, Ps 60:2) is the medieval Hebrew name for Aleppo.

35.note: Joseph ben Judah, the Maghrebi pupil of Maimonides to whom the Guide of the Perplexed is addressed; he settled in Aleppo as a physician. He is "the great physician Rabbi Joseph the Maghrebi" again below.

36.note: The "western lamp" of the Temple lampstand, which, the Talmud says, burned on after the others (b. Shabbat 22b). מַעֲרָבִי "western" is also his name, "the Maghrebi".

37.note: Zech 4:2-3 describes a lampstand with a bowl (גֻּלָּה) on its top and two olive trees beside it. גֻּלָּה "bowl" plays on גּוֹלָה "exile": the two brothers are like the two olive trees, and an ornament to the head of the exile.

38.note: "He" is taken to be the brothers' father (or forebear), Rabbi Nissim; הָרֹאשׁ "the head" may be a title, as in the academies.

39.note: אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים is Ur of the Chaldees (Gen 11:31), read in the Midrash as "the fire of the Chaldees", into which Nimrod threw Abraham, who came out unhurt (Gen. Rabbah 38:13).

40.note: The name Mazhir means "shining", which the line before takes up ("shining like the light of dawn").

41.note: Uncertain. צִיר is both "envoy" (Prov 13:17 "a faithful envoy is healing") and "pang"; read here as "pang". Perhaps "balm for a sick envoy".

42.he: רַבִּי יְשׁוּעָה וְרַבִּי יָכִין הֵם עַמּוּדֵי הַמְּלוּכָה
42.note: Jachin is the name of one of the two pillars of Solomon's Temple (1 Kgs 7:21), hence "the pillars of the kingdom".

43.note: A place after Aleppo on the way to Saruj, not identified with certainty. The word could also be read "westward", but the next line speaks of a congregation "there".

44.note: Saruj (biblical Serug, Gen 11:20), a town in Upper Mesopotamia near Edessa. Aram Naharaim (Gen 24:10), the next stop, is here a city between Saruj and Harran, probably Edessa (al-Ruha); the identification is not certain.

45.he: חַמְדָּן וְיִתְרָן. / רַק פַּגְעִיאֵל בֶּן עָכְרָן
45.note: Biblical names used for their sound: Hemdan and Ithran (Gen 36:26) suggest חֶמְדָּה "delight" and יֶתֶר "abundance"; Pagiel son of Ochran (Num 1:13) suggests פֶּגַע "mishap" and עֹכֵר "troubler".

46.note: A pun: the Talmud tells one to keep fifty cubits away from a תָּם ox, one not yet known to gore (b. Pesahim 112b); תָּם also means "simple, innocent", as the line before calls the scribe.

47.note: Calneh (Gen 10:10, Amos 6:2), one of Nimrod's cities in Shinar. On this route between Harran and Mosul it is probably Raqqa on the Euphrates, which Benjamin of Tudela also calls Calneh.

48.note: Gen 19:1. In rabbinic tradition Sodom is the city that refused charity to the poor; the two generous men are like the two angels who came to Sodom, alone among the close-fisted people of Calneh.

49.note: Ashur (Gen 10:11), the land of Assyria; in medieval Hebrew the city of Mosul on the Tigris, across from the ruins of Nineveh.

50.note: The name Berakhot means "blessings", against which the satire sets his wickedness. In the poem below, בֶּטֶן בְּרָכוֹת can also be heard as "a belly of blessings".

51.note: "Trusty" (נֶאֱמָן) may stand for an Arabic title such as al-Amīn, "the trustworthy"; this is a guess.

52.note: The city is not named. The block ends with Ashur (Isa 27:13), so it may still be Mosul, or a name may have fallen out of the text.

53.note: A town in Iraq ("the land of Shinar", in the lines below) that is not identified with certainty.

54.note: Gen 9:19. The name Noah is explained in Gen 5:29 as "rest" (compare נוּחַ, מָנוֹחַ); the three brothers are the place where the wanderers "find rest".
